subject: Hydra analytics: L0 latency budgeting, scaling options, and cost levers
messages:
From: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.com>
To: Samira Khan <samira@hydraanalytics.com>, Tom Wu <tom.wu@hydraanalytics.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 18 Jul 2027 14:03:00 -0700
Subject: Hydra discovery — L0 latency budgeting, scaling options, and next steps

Hi Samira / Tom —

Thanks for the call earlier — good signal on scope and the 1) latency envelope you want for the L0 call path, 2) concurrent session expectations, and 3) streaming behavior (partial tokens + interleaved tool-calls). Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can size the pilot.

Recap (what we heard)
- Target p95 latency for user-facing L0 responses: ~80–120 ms (token production latency), golden target is 80ms but you mentioned relaxed SLA during peak.
- Expected sustained QPS: 1200 requests/minute (burst to 2.5k/min during morning batch).
- Concurrency model: ~2000 simultaneous open sessions with active KV state; heavy short-lived single-turn queries but occasional multi-turn streaming (avg 3–5 turns).
- Streaming requirement: token-streaming with partial outputs and ability to interleave tool/function calls mid-stream; Stopped-stream fallback acceptable.

Preliminary sizing/constraints from our side
- To meet p95=80ms for typical prompt sizes we expect to recommend a quantized 13B model variant for L0, with continuous batching tuned for 6–10 ms per token overhead and prefix/KV caching for repeated user context.
- For sustained QPS and concurrency above, an autoscale group with reserved baseline (Dedicated) + burst pool provides predictable tail latencies and cost containment.

Cost / performance levers we recommend to prioritize (high level)
1) Continuous batching: reduces per-token overhead at scale — target batching window 5–10ms for interactive workloads.
2) Prefix/KV caching: cache common initial prompts and session KV to avoid re-computation for multi-turn.
3) Quantization profile: 4-bit (QLoRA-style) for the 13B L0 path; allow fallback to 8-bit or full-precision for high-fidelity flows.
4) Model path variants: primary = quantized-13B fast path, fallback = 33B/70B quantized for high-compute-only flows (with higher latency).
5) Smart routing & fallback: route latency-sensitive requests to the Dedicated baseline; route bulk/low-priority to burst/spot capacity.

Attached are two artifacts: 1) hydra-slo-proposal-v2.pdf (simple table mapping SLOs to expected throughput and recommended model variants), 2) hydra-ops-params.xlsx (raw numbers / cost model).

Next steps / asks
- Samira: confirm whether p95=80ms is a hard SLA or an aspirational metric for production.
- Tom: share a representative 30-minute trace (anonymized) or 200 sample requests with token counts so we can run a micro-benchmark.
- Procurement: we may need a short reserved-capacity quote if you prefer baseline Dedicated capacity.
- Redwood: we’ll run a quick perf sweep against your sample set and return a recommended config + cost delta by Wed 21 Jul.

If that matches your understanding I’ll schedule a short runbook sync and hand Ben onto ops sizing and Karthik for model-path decisions.

Thanks —
Hannah
Hannah Schmitt
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Samira Khan <samira@hydraanalytics.com>
To: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Cc: Tom Wu <tom.wu@hydraanalytics.com>
Date: Mon, 19 Jul 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Hydra discovery — L0 latency budgeting, scaling options, and next steps

Thanks Hannah — helpful summary. A couple clarifications from our side: 

1) SLA vs aspirational: For Q3 pilot we can treat 80ms as aspirational; for production (Q4) we want a formal SLA at p95 but negotiable depending on traffic and capacity guarantees.
2) Concurrency: the "2000 sessions" number is a steady-state estimate; peak concurrency may hit ~3500 for a ~20-minute window. We can send an anonymized trace export by EOD.
3) Streaming: yes, we need partial tokens as they arrive; critical for perceived responsiveness. If model switching pauses streaming for >150ms that becomes problematic.

Quick question on your recommendation: when you say quantized-13B for the L0 path, what p95 improvements vs unquantized 13B do you typically observe on our target hardware? Also curious about quality delta for our 2–3 token generation bursts.

Tom — I’ll upload the trace today. Procurement is looped for later.

—Samira
Samira Khan
Head of Product, Hydra Analytics

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: Samira Khan <samira@hydraanalytics.com>, Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Tom Wu <tom.wu@hydraanalytics.com>
Date: Tue, 20 Jul 2027 11:29:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Hydra discovery — L0 latency budgeting, scaling options, and next steps

Appreciate the clarifications Samira — quick answers and plan from ops perspective:

- Perf delta: on our inference profile, 4-bit quantized 13B reduces per-token latency by ~25–40% compared to FP16 13B with negligible quality loss for short 2–5 token bursts in ~70% of prompts. We can provide side-by-side samples on your traces.
- Tail behavior: continuous batching + reserved baseline keeps p95 stable — we recommend reserving baseline capacity to cover the 95th-percentile sustained QPS and using burst pool for spikes.
- Streaming fidelity: model variant switching can be done with session affinity; switching mid-stream introduces a 80–150ms rewarm depending on KV warm cache. To avoid visible pauses we recommend keeping the fast-path model pinned for the session lifecycle where low-latency streaming is critical.

Operational ask list (short)
1) Samira/Tom: upload the 200 sample requests + 1 anonymized 30-min trace to the shared link (or we can accept a dropbox link).
2) Samira: mark which flows are latency-critical vs batch-analytic so we can map to model paths.
3) Procurement: if you want a Dedicated baseline quote, confirm desired monthly commit range (we’ll provision a conservative baseline equal to 110% of 95th percentile).

We’ll run a micro-benchmark Thursday and share a configuration matrix (expected p95, cost delta, and recommended levers) by EOD Fri.

Thanks —
Ben
Ben Carter
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
